title: Space Use Change Associated With Climate Induces Camouflage Mismatch to Increase Extinction Risk in an Endangered Mammal
content:
Camouflage is vital for survival, but climate warming-induced phenological mismatches threaten its efficacy, accelerating extinction risk of small populations. (A) Atmospheric warming and predation suppress (B) populations of endangered Mt. Graham red squirrels. (C) Individuals living at lower population densities are released from territory defense and subsequently increase their home range size. (D) Squirrels with expanded home ranges are poorly camouflaged outside their territory on the forest floor (right squirrel) relative to those that remain in their territory close to their food larders (left squirrel). Ineffective camouflage feeds back to increase hawk predation, initiating a cycle that increasingly exacerbates extinction risk via Allee effects (A–D). Understanding how animals avoid predation can be especially important in conservation during an era of rapid ecological change because predation is a leading factor in maintaining low population sizes.


ABSTRACT

Camouflage is vital for survival, but climate warming may distort the visual environment of predators and prey to reduce crypsis efficacy. Many animals store food using strategies that vary along a continuum from larderhoarding (centralized caching) to scatterhoarding (dispersed caching), and behavioral shifts and space use may help overcome challenges complicated by warming provided that prey remain cryptic. We combined long-term population and behavioral data with comparative analyses of pelage color to assess predation risk in a highly endangered mammal. Environmental warming was associated with decreased population densities, decreased larderhoard use, and expanded space use that reduced camouflage and increased avian predation rates. Integration of long-term demographics with predator-specific visual sensitivities in rapidly changing environments highlights mechanisms underlying population declines that accelerate extinction risk.
